Per-cell QC metrics and outlier flagging

Source: vignettes/qcMetrics.Rmd
qcMetrics.Rmd
library(rscprep)

Two functions, in order. diagnoseQC() calculates the per-cell metrics that filtering decisions get made from; flagQC() marks the cells those metrics say are outliers. Neither one removes anything. The motivation here is that you can look at what a threshold would remove before you actually remove it.

This vignette picks up where mergeSeurat() leaves off:

seurat_list <- seuratFrom10x(manifest = manifest)
seurat_list <- includeMetadata(seurat_list, sample_sheet)
seurat      <- mergeSeurat(seurat_list)

Both functions want that single merged object rather than the list, so that one set of thresholds is chosen from one view of the data.

Calculating the metrics 

seurat <- diagnoseQC(seurat, organism = "mmu")
#> ℹ Diagnosing 1200 cells in assay "RNA" using "mmu" gene patterns.
#> ℹ mito: 8 features matched "^mt".
#> ℹ ribo: 39 features matched "^Rp[sl]".
#> ✔ Added 3 QC metrics to 1200 cells.
#> • pctMito: median 0.95%, max 19.59%
#> • pctRibo: median 4.59%, max 5.91%
#> • log10GenesPerUMI: median 0.764

Three columns land in the metadata, alongside the nCount_RNA and nFeature_RNA that Seurat already wrote:

head(seurat@meta.data[, c("nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA",
                          "pctMito", "pctRibo", "log10GenesPerUMI")])
#>                nCount_RNA nFeature_RNA pctMito pctRibo log10GenesPerUMI
#> Sample_1_Cell1        443          318  15.124   3.612            0.946
#> Sample_1_Cell2        464          326  12.500   3.879            0.943
#> Sample_1_Cell3        444          294  19.595   2.703            0.932
#> Sample_1_Cell4        454          316  15.639   3.304            0.941
  • pctMito: share of a cell’s UMIs coming from mitochondrial genes. High means the cell lost cytoplasmic RNA through a ruptured membrane, so this is the usual first filter. What counts as high is tissue-dependent: 5–10% is a common starting point, but cardiac, muscle and kidney are legitimately mitochondria-rich and a fixed cutoff throws away real cells.
  • pctRibo: share from ribosomal protein genes. Rarely a hard filter, because it varies strongly by cell type. Useful as a comparison between samples that ought to look alike: a sharp shift points at something technical.
  • log10GenesPerUMI: library complexity, log10(nFeature) / log10(nCount). Between 0 and 1 for real cells; low means a library dominated by few transcripts. Around 0.8 is a conventional floor.

The percentages come from matching gene symbols against organism-specific patterns, so organism has to match the data. The package currently supports mouse, rat, human, and zebrafish.

code organism mito ribo
"hsa" human ^MT- ^RP[SL]
"mmu" mouse ^mt ^Rp[sl]
"rno" rat ^Mt- ^Rp[sl]
"dre" zebrafish ^mt- ^rp[sl]

An organism not listed can borrow the code of one whose convention it shares.

Cell cycle, optionally

doCellCycle = TRUE also hands the object to runCellCycle(), adding S.Score, G2M.Score and Phase:

seurat <- diagnoseQC(seurat, organism = "mmu", doCellCycle = TRUE)

It is off by default because, unlike the metrics above, scoring assumes normalized data, and will run Seurat::NormalizeData() on the object itself, with a warning, if it arrives raw.

Flagging outliers

flagQC() marks cells that sit an unusual distance from the rest, using the median absolute deviation rather than a fixed cutoff:

seurat <- flagQC(seurat, metrics = c(nCount_RNA = "lower", pctMito = "higher"))

Each entry is column = bound, and the bound is per metric because which outlier tail matters depends on the metric. nCount_RNA wants "lower": the low tail is empty droplets and dying cells, while the high tail is mostly real, well-captured cells. pctMito wants "higher", since high is bad and low is not. "both" is the default, and is what you want when doublets are the concern.

A MAD-based threshold adapts to the data, which a hard cutoff cannot: a cutoff carried between experiments discards good cells from a shallow run and keeps bad ones from a deep one. The cost is that it assumes most of the cells it is estimated from are good. On a badly failed sample it will call the failure normal and flag the survivors.

Estimating thresholds per sample

This is the argument that matters most. By default flagQC() estimates one threshold across every cell in the object. If your samples differ in sequencing depth (and they usually do), that single threshold describes none of them.

Here are three mouse samples at median depths of roughly 2,500, 6,800 and 25,000 UMIs. Globally:

global <- flagQC(seurat, c(nCount_RNA = "lower", pctMito = "higher"))
#> ℹ Flagging outliers in 2 metrics at 3 MADs from the median (log2 scale), across all cells.
#> ℹ nCount_RNA: 0/1200 cells flagged (0%).
#> • lower: < 87.67 -- 0 cells
#> ℹ pctMito: 68/1200 cells flagged (5.67%).
#> • upper: > 1.386 -- 68 cells

The nCount_RNA threshold comes out at 87 UMIs and catches nothing. Pooling three depth tiers inflates the spread so far that the cutoff falls below every real cell in the experiment, including the dying ones it exists to find.

Now per sample:

seurat <- flagQC(
  seurat,
  metrics  = c(nCount_RNA = "lower", pctMito = "higher"),
  group_by = "Ident"
)
#> ℹ Flagging outliers in 2 metrics at 3 MADs from the median (log2 scale), within 3 groups of Ident.
#> ℹ nCount_RNA: 64/1200 cells flagged (5.33%) across 3 groups.
#> • lower: < 2400-24910 -- 64 cells
#> ℹ pctMito: 62/1200 cells flagged (5.17%) across 3 groups.
#> • upper: > 1.182-1.858 -- 62 cells

Three thresholds instead of one (2,400, 6,512 and 24,910), and the low-count cells in every sample get found. The console prints the range across groups rather than a line per group, so a twenty-sample object stays readable; the per-group numbers are in the table.

"Ident" is the sample name seuratFrom10x() sets, but any discrete metadata column works: a capture batch, a 10x lane, a tissue. Group on the technical variable you want the threshold to absorb.

Note that pctMito barely changed (68 flagged globally, 62 per sample). It is a ratio, so it does not scale with depth. Grouping matters for depth-dependent metrics; for ratio metrics it is close to a no-op. That is worth checking rather than assuming.

Reading the summary

Every call records what it did. getOutlierSummary() reads it back:

qc <- getOutlierSummary(seurat)
qc[, c("metric", "group", "lower", "upper", "n_flagged", "pct_flagged")]
#>       metric    group     lower    upper n_flagged pct_flagged
#> 1 nCount_RNA Sample_1  2400.429       NA        22         5.5
#> 2 nCount_RNA Sample_2  6512.113       NA        12         3.0
#> 3 nCount_RNA Sample_3 24910.163       NA        30         7.5
#> 4    pctMito Sample_1        NA 1.857964        20         5.0
#> 5    pctMito Sample_2        NA 1.431274        12         3.0
#> 6    pctMito Sample_3        NA 1.181886        30         7.5

One row per metric per group. Two things to notice:

  • Thresholds are on the metric’s own scale, even though the estimate was made on a log scale. They can be compared against the column directly.
  • The unenforced tail is NA, not an unapplied number. nCount_RNA was flagged "lower" only, so its upper is blank rather than a cutoff nothing was tested against. The same applies to n_lower / n_upper.

Which sample is losing the most cells?

qc[order(-qc$pct_flagged), c("metric", "group", "n_flagged", "pct_flagged")]
#>       metric    group n_flagged pct_flagged
#> 3 nCount_RNA Sample_3        30         7.5
#> 6    pctMito Sample_3        30         7.5
#> 1 nCount_RNA Sample_1        22         5.5
#> 4    pctMito Sample_1        20         5.0
#> 2 nCount_RNA Sample_2        12         3.0
#> 5    pctMito Sample_2        12         3.0

Repeated calls accumulate into this one table, so an object flagged on counts globally and then on mitochondrial content per sample yields a single table describing both. It is a record written at flag time, not a live view. Cell counts describe the object as it stood then, which is the point, since being able to say afterwards how many cells were dropped and why is the reason to keep it.

Groups too small to estimate from

Per-group estimation creates a failure mode global estimation does not have. A group of two cells has no usable spread, and a group where over half the cells share one value has a MAD of zero. Both are skipped rather than given a meaningless threshold:

seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(nCount_RNA = "lower"), group_by = "Ident")
#> Warning:
#> ! nCount_RNA: no threshold for 1 of 3 Ident groups.
#> ℹ Skipped: tiny (fewer than 3 cells)
#> ✖ Cells in that group are left as NA, not FALSE.
#> ℹ nCount_RNA: 0/58 cells flagged (0%) across 2 groups.

One warning naming every skipped group, not one per group. Skipped groups still get a row in the summary table, with NA thresholds and an NA column, so nothing silently disappears.

That NA-not-FALSE distinction runs throughout. A cell is left NA when it was never judged (missing metric, missing group_by value, or a skipped group), so an unjudged cell is never mistaken for one that passed. It matters at the filtering step below.

Actually filtering

flagQC() writes logical columns and stops. Filtering is yours:

flags <- grep("_outliers$", colnames(seurat@meta.data), value = TRUE)
flags
#> [1] "nCount_RNA_3_lower_outliers" "pctMito_3_higher_outliers"

# `%in% TRUE` treats an unjudged NA as "not an outlier"; use `isTRUE`-style
# logic deliberately rather than letting NA propagate through `|`
keep     <- !Reduce(`|`, lapply(seurat@meta.data[flags], function(x) x %in% TRUE))
filtered <- seurat[, which(keep)]

table(seurat$Ident, keep)
#>           keep
#>            FALSE TRUE
#>   Sample_1    22  378
#>   Sample_2    12  388
#>   Sample_3    30  370

Cross-tabulate before you subset. A sample losing far more than its neighbours is worth understanding rather than filtering: it may have failed, or it may be a genuinely different tissue where the thresholds do not transfer.

You do not have to trust every flag. The columns are independent, so filter on the subset you believe:

filtered <- seurat[, which(!seurat$pctMito_3_higher_outliers %in% TRUE)]

Tuning 

# more aggressive
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(pctMito = "higher"), nmads = 2.5, group_by = "Ident")

# keep all but the extremes
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(pctMito = "higher"), nmads = 5, group_by = "Ident")

# a metric that is already symmetric does not want the log transform
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(log10GenesPerUMI = "lower"), log = FALSE)

nmads is in the column name, so nmads = 3 and nmads = 5 produce separate columns and can be compared side by side. group_by is not in the name, so re-running one metric with different grouping overwrites the previous flags. The summary table is updated to match, so it never describes a column that is no longer there.

log = TRUE is the default and is right for count metrics, which are right-skewed enough that the median and MAD are misleading on the raw scale. Turn it off for anything already roughly symmetric.

Where this leaves you 

seurat <- mergeSeurat(seuratFrom10x(manifest = manifest))
seurat <- diagnoseQC(seurat, organism = "mmu")
seurat <- flagQC(
  seurat,
  metrics  = c(nCount_RNA = "lower", nFeature_RNA = "lower", pctMito = "higher"),
  group_by = "Ident"
)

getOutlierSummary(seurat)          # what would be cut, and from where
write.csv(getOutlierSummary(seurat), "qc/outlier_summary.csv", row.names = FALSE)

Nothing has been removed at this point. The metrics are on the object, the flags are on the object, and the record of how the thresholds were chosen is on the object. Deciding what to drop is the next step, and it is a judgement call, which is why these functions stop short of making it.
